newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK export stocks rally as sterling wobbles.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK export stocks rally as sterling wobbles.

text.p: Signs of weakness in the pound after Britain's change of government proved a welcome relief for shares in British exporters on Friday, after several months when the currency's strength has threatened to squeeze sales margins.

With the pound at one stage down as much as four pfennigs against the mark and two cents against the U.S. dollar in the wake of the Labour Party's election victory, British Steel Plc and other export stocks rebounded sharply from their recent underperformance.

"It is all on the back of the currency," said one market-maker at a leading investment bank. "They have been bombed out on the currency's strength and now they are having a rally on the back of its weakness."

British Steel was the day's biggest gainer amongst FTSE 100 Index stocks, bouncing back from a near three-year low of 137p set on Thursday. By 1435 GMT the share was up 7p or five percent, at 145-1/4.
Other engineering stocks also rose with Siebe Plc up 15 at 932-1/2, TI Group Plc up 11 at 544 and Smiths Industries Plc up 8-1/2 at 766.
Industrial conglomerate BTR Plc was up 7-1/2p at 259-1/2 and aero-engine maker Rolls-Royce Plc was up 2-1/2p at 245.

But sterling recouped some of the early losses as the day progressed and analysts warned that the currency may be underpinned by a prospect of higher UK interest rates, which can boost a currency by luring in a torrent of overseas investment cash in search of high returns.

UK lending rates are expected to be raised at next Wednesday's monetary policy meeting, as the Bank of England battles to cool the pace of growth and prevent inflation. It could be the first of several rate hikes this year.

Analysts also pointed out that forthcoming trading news from leading engineering companies was likely to be loaded with gloomy comments on the impact of the strong pound and today's gains could prove little more than a knee-jerk reaction to recent weakness.

"These shares have been incredibly weak over the last few months," said one analyst, who declined to be named. "But it may be too early to get back in. I suspect (annual meetings) for a lot of engineering companies may still be pretty bad."
"There has to be some fundamental change in the business outlook and that's not there yet," the analyst said. "It could be a bit of a fools' rally."
The strength of sterling in recent months led to a series of profit warnings from a broad range of leading international companies, sapping investment interest.
Most recently Vickers Plc, the tank and Rolls-Royce cars maker, warned last month that export orders were proving harder to obtain and the profit margins on them was tending to narrow.
Vickers was up 2-1/2p at 215 on Friday.
Currency dealers said a report in national newspaper The Times had helped fuel the post-election decline in the pound.
The paper said that unless the new government did something to bring the exchange rate to heel the government would be destoyed by an eventual humiliating devaluation.
It urged tax increases rather than higher rates to take the heat out of the economy.
Yet forex experts said that for the time being the underlying factors that had boosted the currency by some 25 percent against the mark since last August remained in place.

"Unless there is a fundamental change in the policies the Labour Party proposed before the election, the pound is likely to recover," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at investment bank UBS.
Towards the close of stock market business on Friday, sterling had pared its early decline to be down less than one pfennig against the mark and less than a cent against the dollar.
